40840: A parent's school of wisdom for life in God's world: short, sharp sayings on speech, work, money, family and justice, all rooted in reverence for the LORD.
40841: Solomon, 'the wise', Hezekiah's scribes, Agur and Lemuel

40844: Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes (traditionally Solomonic)
40846: Jerusalem royal court and scribal circles
40847: The collections point to the royal court (sayings about kings, Prov 25:2-7) and to family teaching. Final editing probably took place in Jerusalem after the exile.
40848: 'My son': young men being trained for adult responsibility, and through them all Israel
40849: Households and scribal schools in Judah
40850: Proverbs is framed as a father and mother teaching a son as he steps into adult life: choosing friends, handling money, resisting seduction and speaking wisely. The 'son' becomes a stand-in for every reader.
40851: The Egyptian *Instruction of Amenemope*, thirty chapters of advice from a scribe to his son, is probably composed in the Ramesside period (dating approximate).
40852: Solomon's court in Jerusalem gains an international reputation for wisdom (1 Kgs 4:29-34; 1 Kgs 10:1-9).
40853: Hezekiah's scribes copy and arrange a further collection of Solomon's proverbs (Prov 25:1).
40854: Many scholars date the introductory chapters (Prov 1-9) and final editing to the Persian period.

40856:
Every ancient Near Eastern civilisation had wisdom literature. Egyptian 'instructions' were written by officials and kings for their sons; Mesopotamian scribes collected proverbs and advice. Israel's sages took part in this international conversation. The clearest example is Prov 22:17-24:22. In 1924 the Egyptologist Adolf Erman showed that many lines closely match the *Instruction of Amenemope*, and he suggested that an obscure Hebrew word in Prov 22:20 should be read *sheloshim*, 'thirty', matching Amenemope's thirty chapters (many translations now print 'thirty sayings'). Scholars still debate the direction and nature of the borrowing, but most accept a real connection.

What Israel did with this material matters more than where it came from. Proverbs grounds all wisdom in 'the fear of the LORD' (Prov 1:7; Prov 9:10), using Israel's covenant name for God. Practical skill, such as how to answer an angry person (Prov 15:1) or manage a field (Prov 24:30-34), is treated as part of living faithfully before the Creator who built the world by wisdom (Prov 3:19-20).

The book has two main types of material. Chapters 1-9 are longer speeches by a parent and by personified Wisdom, a woman calling in the streets, competing with Folly for the young man's attention. Chapters 10-29 are mostly two-line sayings, often contrasting the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool, the diligent and the lazy. Chapters 30-31 bring in foreign voices and end with a poem about a 'woman of strength'.

Proverbs are not laws or promises. They are generalisations: observations about how life usually works in God's ordered world. The book itself places contradictory-seeming proverbs side by side (Prov 26:4-5) to train judgement about which one fits which situation.
40858: 'Hear, my son, your father's instruction, and forsake not your mother's teaching' (Prov 1:8). Education happened in the household. The mother's role in teaching is unusual in ancient wisdom texts and stands out in Israel's version.
40860: Wisdom is pictured as a noble woman who builds a house, prepares a banquet and invites the simple; Folly is a loud woman who invites them to stolen water and death. The young man must choose whose house he enters.
40862: Wisdom says she was with the LORD before creation, like a master craftsman or delighted child beside him (the Hebrew *amon* is uncertain). This poem shaped Jewish ideas of Torah as the blueprint of the world and Christian ideas of Christ as God's wisdom.
40864: Reputation was a household's wealth. Proverbs repeatedly warns about gossip, quarrels, flattery and lies, because speech built or destroyed honour within the community.
40866: Elders sat at the gate to judge disputes. The capable woman's husband is known there, and Wisdom calls out there; it is the public square of honour.
40867: Proverbs is not only about personal success. It warns against moving boundary stones, bribery and oppressing the poor, whose defender is God himself.
40868:
In Jewish tradition Wisdom in Proverbs became closely identified with the Torah. Ben Sira (chapter 24) and later rabbis read Prov 8 as describing Torah as God's companion at creation; *Genesis Rabbah* 1:1 opens by reading the uncertain word *amon* in Prov 8:30 as 'artisan' or 'tool', so that God looked into the Torah as an architect looks at a plan when creating the world. When the Torah scroll is returned to the ark in synagogue, the congregation sings Prov 3:17-18, 'She is a tree of life to those who grasp her ... her ways are ways of pleasantness', applying Wisdom's words to the Torah itself.

On Friday evenings many Jewish homes sing *Eshet Hayil*, 'A woman of valour' (Prov 31:10-31), in honour of the wife and mother before the Sabbath meal. Rabbinic and later Jewish readings also took the poem allegorically, of the Torah, the Sabbath or the Divine Presence, but its main life is as a family blessing.

Read within the covenant, Proverbs shows what living as God's people looks like on an ordinary Tuesday. It hardly mentions the exodus, the temple or the covenant at Sinai, yet its 'fear of the LORD' uses the covenant name and its values echo Deuteronomy: honest weights (Prov 11:1; Deut 25:13-16), care for the poor and orphans, faithfulness in marriage. Wisdom is not a self-help path apart from relationship with God; it is the fruit of trusting him with the whole of life (Prov 3:5-6).
40870: The book exists to give wisdom to the simple and the young; its root is the fear of the LORD.
40872: Ten parental speeches warn against violent gangs and seduction, while Lady Wisdom and Woman Folly compete for the son.
40874: Hundreds of two-line contrasts about the righteous and wicked, the wise and foolish, in speech, work and money.
40875: Thirty sayings with close Egyptian parallels, then more sayings of the wise.
40877: More Solomonic proverbs with vivid images from farm, court and home, including the 'answer a fool' pair.
40879: A foreign sage confesses he lacks understanding and lists numerical sayings drawn from nature.
40881: A queen mother teaches her son to defend the poor, and an alphabetic poem praises the woman of strength who fears the LORD.
40901: A comparison, saying or parable; something that 'stands for' something else. The title of the book is *Mishlei*, 'proverbs of'.
40902: Skill, whether of a craftsman, a sailor or a ruler; in Proverbs, skill in living well before God.
40903: Reverent awe that shapes behaviour: taking God seriously as Creator and covenant Lord. It is the starting point and first principle of wisdom.
40905: Not someone of low intelligence but someone morally closed, who will not take correction. Proverbs distinguishes the naive (*peti*), the fool and the scoffer (*lets*).
40907: *Hayil* means strength, capability, even military valour. The same phrase describes Ruth (Ruth 3:11).
40908: Kings presents Solomon as the model wise king and author of thousands of proverbs, and then shows his later folly.
40909: Job and Ecclesiastes test the edges of Proverbs' patterns; all three share the conclusion that wisdom begins with fearing God.
40910: In the Hebrew Bible Ruth follows Proverbs; Ruth is the only person called an 'eshet hayil', a living example of Prov 31.
40911: James is often called the New Testament's wisdom book, with Proverbs-like teaching on the tongue, humility and wisdom from above. James 4:6 quotes Prov 3:34.
40912: Paul calls Christ 'the wisdom of God', drawing on the figure of Wisdom in Proverbs.
40913: Paul quotes Prov 25:21-22 on feeding your enemy and heaping burning coals on his head.
40914: Jesus taught like a sage, in short sayings and parables (the Hebrew *mashal* covers both), and claimed that 'something greater than Solomon is here' (Matt 12:42). New Testament writers drew on the figure of Wisdom with God at creation to describe Christ: 'the wisdom of God' (1 Cor 1:24), the one 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom' (Col 2:3), the Word through whom all things were made (John 1:1-3; compare Prov 8:22-31). In the fourth century Arius used Prov 8:22 ('the LORD created me') to argue that the Son was created, which shows how influential the passage was; Nicene writers answered that it describes Wisdom's role, not the Son's origin. Jewish tradition reads the same poem of the Torah, not of a person.
40916: 'Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old he will not depart from it' (Prov 22:6) is a promise: if parents do it right, their children will stay faithful. Similarly, honouring God with wealth guarantees full barns (Prov 3:9-10).
40917: Proverbs are generalisations about how life usually works, not covenant promises or legal contracts. The book itself shows this by placing opposite sayings together (Prov 26:4-5) and by acknowledging that the righteous sometimes suffer and the wicked prosper (Prov 16:8; Prov 28:6). Scholars such as Tremper Longman, Michael Fox and Bruce Waltke all stress the difference between a proverb and a promise.
40918: Evangelical scholars agree almost universally on this point; it is a popular misreading rather than a scholarly debate. They add that proverbs are still reliably true as patterns: good parenting really does tend to shape children, and wise living generally leads to flourishing. The proverbs are not false when exceptions occur; they were never meant to cover every case.
40919: Treating proverbs as guarantees burdens grieving parents with false guilt and turns faith into a formula. Reading them as wisdom frees them to guide without condemning.
40920: Proverbs 31 as a checklist for wives

40922: The poem is an alphabetic acrostic, a celebration from A to Z, not a job description. In Jewish homes it is sung as praise to the wife, not as a test. Many scholars note that it also presents Lady Wisdom in household form, closing the book as Prov 1-9 opened it, and that the woman is a capable trader, landowner and teacher, not a narrow domestic figure.
40923: Complementarian evangelical teachers often still see in her a model of godly womanhood and household leadership; egalitarian evangelicals stress her economic independence. Both agree her central quality is that she 'fears the LORD' (Prov 31:30), which applies to men and women alike.
40924: A checklist reading can crush women with impossible standards; a praise reading invites honouring the faithful women already present.
40925: Proverbs trained Israel's young people, officials and households to live as God's people in daily affairs: speaking truthfully, working faithfully, keeping marriage, protecting the poor and respecting authority, all under the fear of the LORD.
40926: It remains one of the most practical books of the Bible for work, money, friendship, parenting and speech. Read as wisdom rather than formula, it builds judgement and character instead of rule-keeping or anxiety.
40927: A royal teacher tests every road to lasting gain, finds that life slips through our fingers like breath, and concludes that we should receive each day's food, work and love as God's gift and fear him.
40928: Qohelet ('the Gatherer' or 'the Teacher'), presented by a frame narrator
40929: The main speaker calls himself Qohelet, 'son of David, king in Jerusalem'. The name comes from *qahal*, 'assembly', and means something like 'one who gathers' (people or sayings). A second voice, the editor, introduces him and sums up at the end (Eccl 12:9-14).
40930: The book never names Solomon, but the royal experiments in Eccl 1:12-2:26 clearly wear Solomon's robes. The Hebrew is late, close to the Hebrew of the Mishnah, with Aramaic influence and probably Persian loanwords; for this reason most scholars, including conservatives such as Franz Delitzsch and Tremper Longman, think 'Solomon' is a literary persona chosen by a later sage. Others, such as Walter Kaiser and Duane Garrett, have defended Solomonic authorship.
40931: The speaker presents himself as king in Jerusalem. A Persian or early Hellenistic date would make the writer a Jerusalem sage living under foreign rule.
40932: Educated, reflective Israelites, and especially young people deciding what to live for
40933: On a later dating, Judah was a small province under Persian or Ptolemaic rule, where a commercial economy, taxes and officials created new wealth and new anxiety (Eccl 5:8-9; Eccl 5:10-12). Many asked what lasting 'profit' (*yitron*, a business word) human effort could secure.
40934: Persia conquers Babylon; Judah becomes a province of a vast commercial empire with coinage and taxation.
40935: Alexander the Great takes the Levant; Greek ideas begin to spread across the region.
40936: Judah passes under the Ptolemies of Egypt, known for efficient tax-farming (dating of Ecclesiastes to this era is one common view).
40937: Fragments of Ecclesiastes later found at Qumran (4QQoh-a) date to around 175-150 BC, setting a latest possible date for the book.
40938:
Ecclesiastes is the Bible's most unsettling book, and that is the point. Its key word, *hevel*, appears about 38 times. Older translations render it 'vanity', meaning 'emptiness'; the Hebrew literally means 'breath' or 'vapour', something real but fleeting and impossible to grasp. The opening cry 'hevel of hevels' (Eccl 1:2) is a superlative, like 'holy of holies': utterly fleeting, completely beyond our grip.

Qohelet describes a royal experiment. He tries wisdom, pleasure, great building projects, wealth and achievement (Eccl 2:1-11), and each time he asks what 'gain' remains. His answer is that nothing lasts 'under the sun', a phrase used about 29 times for life seen from the ground level of ordinary human experience. Death takes the wise and the fool alike (Eccl 2:14-16); injustice sits in the courts (Eccl 3:16); the righteous sometimes die young while the wicked live long (Eccl 7:15). He refuses to pretend otherwise.

Yet a second refrain runs through the book. Seven times Qohelet commends joy: eat your bread, drink your wine, enjoy life with the one you love, do your work with all your might, because these are God's gift (Eccl 2:24-26; Eccl 3:12-13; Eccl 5:18-20; Eccl 8:15; Eccl 9:7-10; Eccl 11:9-10). The answer to life's fleetingness is not despair but gratitude, receiving each day rather than trying to master it.

Scholars disagree on how the voices fit together. Some read Qohelet as a sceptic whose views the editor corrects in the epilogue. Others, like Michael Fox, see a coherent thinker honestly facing contradictions. Others, like Craig Bartholomew, read the book as a journey in which 'under the sun' observation alternates with gaps of faith ('remember your Creator', Eccl 12:1) until the editor's conclusion: fear God and keep his commandments (Eccl 12:13).
40940: Life viewed from within the world of human experience, without a view from heaven. Qohelet asks what we can know and gain from observation alone.
40942: Qohelet uses economic words: *yitron* (profit, surplus) and *heleq* (portion, share). Lasting profit is impossible, but each person does receive a portion from God to enjoy now.
40944: Ancient Near Eastern literature includes 'royal autobiographies' in which a king boasts of his deeds. Qohelet imitates the genre and then deflates it: all his achievements are breath.
40946: Israel's common picture of death was Sheol, a shadowy place of silence. Qohelet stresses that all go to one place and that no one knows what comes after, so we must live now.
40948: Clean clothes, oil on the head, bread and wine were signs of festival and celebration. Qohelet commends them as fitting responses to God's gift of life.
40950: Eccl 12:1-7 describes ageing and death with a series of images: the keepers of the house trembling (hands), the grinders ceasing (teeth), the silver cord snapped. Ancient and modern readers have decoded it in different ways.
40951:
Ecclesiastes is one of the five *Megillot* (scrolls) read in the synagogue year. It is read at Sukkot, the Feast of Booths, usually on the Sabbath during the festival. The pairing is deliberate: Sukkot is called 'the season of our rejoicing', a harvest festival when Israel was commanded to rejoice (Deut 16:13-15) while living in flimsy temporary huts. A book about life's fleetingness is read in the fragile *sukkah* at the moment of fullest abundance, reminding Israel that every harvest is a gift and every shelter temporary. Some explain the reading as a check on the wealth of harvest time.

The rabbis argued about the book. The Mishnah records disagreement between the schools of Shammai and Hillel over whether Ecclesiastes 'defiles the hands', that is, counts as holy Scripture (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5; Eduyot 5:3). The Talmud reports that the sages wanted to withdraw it because its words seemed to contradict each other, but kept it because it begins and ends with words of Torah (Shabbat 30b). The Midrash *Kohelet Rabbah* reads the book as Solomon's words and often finds in its 'under the sun' the contrast with Torah, which is 'above the sun'.

Read within the covenant, the book's final word ties its searching to Israel's life with God: 'fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of a person' (Eccl 12:13). Its emphasis on receiving food, drink, work and love with joy also echoes the Torah's festival commands. Qohelet is honest about death and injustice in the way Job and the laments are honest, but he keeps speaking within the frame of a God who gives, judges and is to be feared.
40953: The motto, and a poem on endless cycles of sun, wind and rivers where nothing new happens.
40955: Qohelet tests wisdom, pleasure, building and wealth; nothing yields lasting gain, but eating and working with joy is God's gift.
40957: God has set times for birth and death, weeping and dancing, and put eternity in human hearts without letting us see the whole.
40959: Oppression, envy, lonely labour, politics and religion done carelessly; better two than one, better listening than many words.

40967: A poem on youth, old age and death; the editor concludes: fear God and keep his commandments, for God will judge.

41002: Both books challenge a tidy view of reward and punishment and end with God's sovereignty and human reverence.

41005: Christian readers have often treated Ecclesiastes as the honest question to which the resurrection is God's answer. Paul says creation was subjected to 'futility' (the Septuagint's word for *hevel*) 'in hope' of liberation (Rom 8:20-21), and he ends his great resurrection chapter by saying that labour in the Lord is 'not in vain' (1 Cor 15:58), as if speaking straight to Qohelet's question about lasting gain. Jesus' teaching on not storing up treasures that moth and rust destroy (Matt 6:19-21) and his parable of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21) echo Ecclesiastes closely. Jewish readers, by contrast, see the book's answer in the fear of God and the commandments, and in receiving life's joys within the Torah's festivals. Both read the book as clearing away false hopes.
